current_criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s description of living beings (humans, animals) or their contextual interactions is contextually reasonable and grounded in the visual evidence — but ONLY after the answer has been confirmed to be factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Plausibility is strictly a tiebreaker for factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and is inapplicable if either candidate is factually incorrect or visually ungrounded. It must be based solely on observable visual cues and real-world biological/physical plausibility — no speculation, external knowledge, or aesthetic judgment is permitted. Plausibility does not apply to non-living subjects (e.g., statues, logos, abstract art, objects), abstract representations, or spatial arrangements unless they imply biological or physical impossibility (e.g., a giraffe in a cage). When visual evidence supports an emotional or behavioral inference (e.g., open mouth, raised arms, smiling, frowning), such terms are valid under plausibility — as long as they are directly grounded in observable visual cues (e.g., relaxed posture, stern expression). Contextually reasonable behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘arrogant’, ‘serious’, ‘playful’, ‘browsing’) are acceptable if visually supported — even if subjective — and should not be penalized. Plausibility is not a tool to reward minimalism or penalize contextual detail — it is strictly for rejecting falsehoods in behavior or context. It does not apply to social norms or cultural expectations unless directly supported by visual evidence — and should not penalize workers for making reasonable behavioral interpretations. Plausibility is not a substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified regardless of plausibility. The criterion is strictly for inferred behavior, not event type or setting — any suggestion of a setting (e.g., ‘stage’, ‘competition’) that contradicts the visual context is a violation — unless directly supported by visual cues (e.g., stage lights, podium, audience). Directional or spatial qualifiers (e.g., ‘toward the left’, ‘extended forward’) are allowed if visually supported — they are not speculative if grounded. Plausibility is inapplicable for non-living subjects — such answers are evaluated under other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency). If the criterion is inapplicable, preference must be determined by other applicable criteria — not by defaulting to caution or omitting details. Annotators must never use plausibility to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported inferences — these are penalized under visual grounding and factual consistency. Descriptive accuracy (e.g., ‘legs bent’, ‘arms extended’) is not penalized as ‘redundant’ or ‘misleading’ if it is visually supported and biologically plausible — and must be rewarded. Plausibility is not a tiebreaker for non-living subjects — it applies only to living beings or their interactions — and must be evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed. Plausibility does not evaluate descriptive style — only factual accuracy, visual grounding, and biological reasonableness — and ‘simpler’ does not equate to ‘more plausible’. The criterion must be applied only to affirmative, visually grounded descriptions — not to denials or negative claims — and plausibility should never be used to evaluate or override factual consistency or to resolve ties involving factually incorrect answers. Plausibility is not a preference rule — it is a verification filter for contextual reasonableness in living beings only — and must not be used to override or justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported inferences.

current_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty_in_ambiguous_scenes
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer appropriately expresses uncertainty only when visual evidence is genuinely ambiguous, occluded, low-resolution, or insufficient to support definitive claims — and only after the answer has been verified as factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. It does not apply to hallucinated, misidentified, or factually incorrect answers — which are always disqualified under visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. Annotators must first confirm visual grounding and factual consistency — if either is violated, this criterion is inapplicable. Calibrated uncertainty is rewarded when the answer uses cautious language (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘appears to be’, ‘not clearly visible’) to acknowledge ambiguity — but only when the visual evidence truly lacks clarity (e.g., partially obscured objects, indistinct textures, or unresolvable spatial relationships). It is not a substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency — and must never be used to mask hallucinations, misrepresentations, or unsupported claims. Uncertainty is not penalized for describing clearly visible elements — even if their identity is contextually open (e.g., ‘a red object’ is acceptable; ‘a red object with a face’ is only acceptable if facial features are visually supported). The criterion applies only to visual ambiguity — not to interpretive, emotional, or contextual inferences that are grounded in visible cues (e.g., ‘smiling’ is acceptable if a smile is visible; ‘curious’ is acceptable if posture implies curiosity and is visually supported). It does not penalize accurate, specific descriptions of clearly visible elements — even if they are non-central to the question. Uncertainty is never rewarded for vague or unnecessary language — it is only appropriate when the visual record is genuinely insufficient. It does not apply to questions requiring absolute certainty (e.g., object identification in clear images) — and does not penalize confident claims in such cases. Hallucinated or unsupported claims — even if framed with uncertainty — are always penalized. The goal is to reward cautious, contextually appropriate language in ambiguous visual contexts — while prioritizing visual fidelity, factual accuracy, and descriptive precision over vague or overcautious interpretations.

current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Completeness is evaluated ONLY for answers that are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — any answer containing hallucinations, misidentifications, or direct visual contradictions is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation, regardless of detail level. Completeness measures whether the answer includes all visually present elements that are semantically required to fully answer the question’s literal intent — defined as elements directly necessary to satisfy the question’s core factual demand (e.g., object identity, spatial relationships, posture, motion, or contextually grounded actions). Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency — if either is violated, completeness is inapplicable. If an answer is factually consistent, completeness is judged by whether it covers all semantically essential visual components — not all visible details, nor aesthetic descriptors, nor speculative inferences — and omission of clearly visible, semantically essential elements (e.g., posture when asked ‘what is the person doing?’) is penalized. Adding non-essential, hallucinated, or contextually unsupported details (e.g., ‘a camel’ not visible) does not improve completeness — it reduces quality. Completeness does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) unless they are visually grounded and semantically relevant to answering the question — and even then, they are not required. Completeness is not about verbosity or exhaustive listing — it is about covering only the essential visual components required to fully answer the question’s literal intent. If two answers are factually consistent, the one that includes more semantically essential, visually present elements wins — but only if those elements are not hallucinated. Completeness is never used to override factual consistency — factual consistency is the non-negotiable prerequisite. If an answer is factually inconsistent, it cannot be considered complete, regardless of its detail level. Completeness is evaluated only after factual consistency is confirmed — and only among factually consistent answers. Annotators must reject any answer that contains factual errors for completeness evaluation, and instead evaluate it based on factual consistency first. The criterion does not apply to open-ended, interpretive, or aesthetic questions — in which case, visual grounding and factual consistency are the only evaluation criteria. Completeness should not be used to penalize accurate but non-critical details — e.g., background colors or subtle textures — unless they are essential to answering the question’s intent. If the question does not require object identification or description, then object details are not essential — and omitting them does not constitute incompleteness. The goal is to ensure that factually correct answers are complete in their coverage of the question’s core intent, without over-rewarding detail or penalizing accurate but peripheral descriptions. Examples: For ‘What is the person doing?’, ‘standing’ is essential; ‘wearing a red shirt’ is non-essential unless the question asks about clothing. For ‘What is in the foreground?’, omitting a visible object is incomplete; for ‘What is the object?’, omitting visible shape or color is incomplete if those are essential to identification. Completeness does not reward speculative or non-visual inferences — e.g., ‘in a warehouse’ is allowed if visually supported, but ‘has a secret code’ is hallucinated and disqualifies the answer. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must not penalize for minor factual errors (e.g., color misidentification) if the core object or action is correctly described and visually grounded. Completeness is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent answers — but it should not be used to penalize minor factual errors that do not undermine the overall factual consistency or visual grounding. Finally, completeness does not apply to questions where the context is not visually relevant (e.g., team identification, jersey norms) unless explicitly required by the question’s intent. The criterion must explicitly define 'semantically essential' as elements required by the question’s literal intent — not architectural or structural features — and must clarify that contextual, non-essential details (like a Coca-Cola box) are still 'complete' if visually present, and that omitting such elements does not constitute incompleteness unless they are directly relevant to answering the question. It must also explicitly exclude architectural elements from being considered 'essential' unless the question is about room structure or layout. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only evaluated for factually consistent answers — and that if both candidates are factually inconsistent, neither is eligible for completeness evaluation — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). It must also clarify that a factual error (like misidentifying color) disqualifies an answer from completeness evaluation, regardless of how well it describes other visible elements. Additionally, the criterion should specify that if one answer is factually consistent and the other is not, the consistent one should be preferred — but if both are factually inconsistent, completeness is not applicable and the worker must rely on other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only applicable when the question’s literal intent requires specific visual elements beyond simple count or identification — e.g., spatial arrangement, functional use, or configuration — and must not penalize omissions of non-essential details (like spatial distribution) when the core factual requirement (e.g., count) is satisfied. It must also explicitly state that 'semantically essential' elements are defined only within the context of factually correct answers — and that any claim that is factually wrong (even if more specific) is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. The criterion must explicitly prohibit rewarding speculative or contextually inferred arrangements that are not visually supported — even if they seem ‘semantically essential’. It must clarify that completeness only applies to literal, factual descriptions — not interpretive or inferred structures — and must penalize any answer that misrepresents the visual arrangement, even if it seems plausible. The criterion should also specify that ‘semantically essential’ elements must be visually present or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues — not speculative reconstruction — and must not reward hallucinated structures even if they seem ‘logical’ or ‘contextually appropriate’. Finally, it should clarify that completeness does not apply to questions asking for ‘how’ or ‘why’ — which might imply interpretation — and must be strictly applied to literal, factual descriptions. The criterion must explicitly state that 'semantically required' elements are defined by the question’s literal intent, not by contextual or interpretive assumptions. It must also clarify that adding non-essential, visually present details is not a strength under completeness — and that factual consistency is a non-negotiable prerequisite. Furthermore, the criterion should warn annotators that 'semantically required' does not mean 'contextually relevant' or 'socially appropriate' — and that visual presence alone is insufficient if the element is not required by the question. Finally, the criterion must explicitly forbid using completeness to override factual consistency — and must clarify that if one answer is hallucinated, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of detail level. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness rewards inclusion of all visually present, semantically essential elements — not omitting them for stylistic or aesthetic reasons. It must clarify that 'essential' means necessary for answering the question's literal intent — not minimal or concise. The description should penalize omission of visually present elements unless they are irrelevant to the question — and must explicitly forbid penalizing accurate, visually grounded details for being 'non-essential' or 'non-critical' unless they are genuinely irrelevant. The criterion should also clarify that 'completeness' is not about conciseness or accuracy of terminology — only about covering the visually necessary elements. Finally, it should explicitly warn against penalizing answers for including visually present, semantically relevant details that are not required for literal accuracy — even if they are not the most 'precise' or 'concise'.

current_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
current_criteria.description: The answer must align precisely with the visually verifiable elements present in the image — no fabrication, misidentification, omission of clearly visible elements, or misrepresentation of spatial, structural, or visual attributes is permitted. Annotators evaluate whether every claimed visual detail (objects, positions, colors, textures, labels, spatial relationships, and micro-details) is directly supported by what is visibly present. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., blurry text, partially obscured objects), the answer may express calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly 5 pillows') — but must not fabricate or omit elements that are clearly visible. Omitting visible elements is a factual inconsistency unless those elements are explicitly irrelevant to the question. The criterion applies only to observable, static, geometric, or structural visual cues — motion blur, implied motion, or contextual inferences (e.g., 'warehouse from shelves') are not grounds for factual inconsistency if they do not contradict visible structure. Hallucinations include adding nonexistent objects, misidentifying existing ones, or claiming actions not visually supported — even if plausible. Factual consistency does not require pixel-perfect accuracy or exhaustive detail — only that claims match the visual record. Subjective inferences (e.g., 'calm,' 'arrogant') or aesthetic judgments are not hallucinations unless they imply a fabricated visual attribute. Contextual or inferential claims are permitted if visually plausible and do not contradict the image. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for opinions, interpretations, or non-visual metadata (e.g., artist names, titles). When two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers are applied based on completeness or specificity — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge, and must reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable.' Additionally, the criterion explicitly clarifies: (1) Denying the presence of an object is factually consistent if that object is not visually present; omitting other visible objects is not a factual inconsistency unless those objects are directly relevant to answering the question; (2) Factual consistency is evaluated for each specific claim — not for completeness of the entire scene — and hallucinations (misidentifications) are penalized even if other elements are omitted or inaccurately described; (3) Subjective interpretations of visual arrangement (e.g., 'chaotic spacing', 'orderly formation') are permitted as long as they do not contradict the visible structure — and are not penalized as factual inconsistencies; (4) Factual consistency does not penalize detail accuracy or completeness — only hallucinations, misidentifications, or omissions of clearly visible elements; (5) Visible elements, even if minor or non-central, are essential to factual consistency — and omitting them (especially if they are directly observable) constitutes a factual inconsistency; (6) Factual consistency applies only to visual elements — not titles, artist names, or metadata — and visual elements must be confirmed against the image, not external knowledge; (7) Subjective or stylistic visual attributes (like 'red cheeks') are not hallucinations if they are visually supported; (8) 'Factual consistency' does not apply to non-visual elements — which are evaluated under other criteria — to avoid confusion and misapplication; (9) Relative size or spatial descriptors (e.g., 'small portion,' 'most of the space') are acceptable as long as they are visually accurate — and 'small' does not imply hallucination if the object occupies a portion of the frame; (10) Structural or spatial claims (e.g., 'on shelves' vs. 'hanging from ceiling') must be visually verifiable — and any inference contradicting clear visual structure is a factual inconsistency; (11) Factual consistency requires accurate description of individual visual states when multiple subjects or varying conditions exist — not overgeneralization; (12) Answers must match the specific term requested in the question (e.g., 'English language term'), even if a different term is visually accurate or commonly used — but functional or contextual descriptions are allowed if they are non-visual and non-hallucinated; (13) Factual consistency requires reporting all clearly visible elements — not just avoiding fabrication — and 'unclear' only applies to ambiguous visual cues, not to cases where elements are clearly present but miscounted or misidentified; (14) Omitting visible elements — even if the worker is unsure about their role — is a factual inconsistency, and the number of visible elements must be accurately reported unless explicitly ambiguous (e.g., 'blurry', 'partially obscured'); (15) Adding non-essential, accurate details (e.g., background color, posture, facial expression) is acceptable and does not constitute factual inconsistency; (16) Hallucinations include not only adding nonexistent objects but also misidentifying or misrepresenting visible elements — such as claiming an object is 'revealing his upper body' when the visual evidence shows he is wearing a shirt; (17) Descriptions of visual elements that are inherently stylized, symbolic, or graphic — including implied motion or action — are acceptable as long as they are not hallucinations; (18) Factual consistency does not penalize accurate, non-hallucinated details — even if they are non-essential or redundant — as long as they are visually supported; (19) The criterion explicitly distinguishes between visually verifiable elements and inferred context — penalizing only when inferred claims contradict visual evidence — and must clarify that calibrated uncertainty should not be used to justify unsupported inferences; (20) Factual consistency does not prohibit reasonable, non-hallucinated inferences about behavior, threat, or context — as long as they are grounded in the visible subject’s state and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (21) The criterion must be revised to clarify that 'factual consistency' applies only to observable, structural, or geometric visual cues — not to abstract or interpretive descriptions — and that aesthetic or compositional terms (e.g., 'scattered', 'concentrated') are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual evidence; (22) Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record and must be respected — and factual consistency requires matching claims to all visual cues — including labels, even if they are stylized or child-like — and not just to visual objects or structure; (23) The absence of a label does not imply a claim is hallucinated — and labeled elements must be verified as visually present, not inferred or imagined; (24) If an element is labeled in the image, its description must be factually consistent — even if the label is ambiguous or artistic — and that labels should not be ignored or overruled by other visual cues unless the label contradicts the visual record.

current_criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
current_criteria.description: Multimodal_coherence evaluates the internal consistency and visual fidelity of an answer’s claims — specifically, whether all stated visual elements (objects, actions, spatial relations, postures, inferred states) are either directly visible or conservatively inferred from unambiguous visual cues — and ONLY applies when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding: if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation. The criterion does NOT penalize factual errors, hallucinations, or misidentifications — those are handled by visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. It is a downstream refinement for factually correct answers only — not a tiebreaker or primary filter. When evaluating, annotators must: (a) confirm factual consistency and visual grounding first — if violated, multimodal_coherence is irrelevant; (b) check for internal contradictions (e.g., ‘standing on a curved track’ while the image shows a straight path); (c) verify that inferred actions or states are grounded in observable posture, motion, or context (e.g., ‘drinking from a bowl’ is inferable from posture, but ‘browsing Apple web pages’ is hallucinated unless Apple logos are visible); (d) penalize unsupported speculation — even if plausible — and reward only conservative, visually supported inferences. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with fewer contradictions or more conservative inferences is preferred — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Multimodal_coherence does not evaluate linguistic style, completeness, plausibility, or aesthetic judgment — only strict fidelity to the visual record. It is not a tiebreaker for hallucinated or denied elements — those are handled by visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. Visual confirmation is sufficient when an object is clearly identifiable — even if its exact type is not — and should not penalize accurate descriptions of visible objects that are not perfectly certain in their type. ‘Conservative inference’ applies only when visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — not when it is present but not fully clear. Descriptions of visible elements (even stylized or abstract) are not hallucinations if they are factually consistent — and should be reported without penalty. Spatial relationships like ‘beneath’ or ‘under’ are not hallucinations if they are visually supported by the image’s perspective — even if not immediately obvious. Non-living or static objects (e.g., statues) may be described with posture descriptions (e.g., ‘bent legs’) as long as they are visually grounded — regardless of biological plausibility. ‘Pattern’ is not a hallucination if it accurately describes a human image — and should not be penalized unless misrepresented (e.g., a photo misidentified as a ‘logo’ or ‘symbol’ without visual support). Color variations that are visually supported (e.g., ‘green’, ‘turquoise’, ‘blue-green’) are not hallucinations — and should not be penalized. Text labels within the image are part of the visual evidence — and descriptive phrases matching labels are not hallucinations — they are rewarded. Hallucinations are only penalized when the claim contradicts verifiable visual evidence — not when the answer adds detail. ‘Unsupported speculation’ applies only to claims that misrepresent the image’s structure or content — not to accurate but non-essential details. ‘Conservative inference’ is not a justification for omitting visible elements — only for handling ambiguity. Visual evidence includes pixels, clear outlines, distinguishable symbols — and annotators must verify presence before applying ‘conservative inference’. The criterion must not penalize accurate but more detailed descriptions when they are visually supported. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., whether banana is ‘at the bottom’), a descriptive, non-inferential answer is preferred over speculative reconstruction — but only if the ambiguity is not resolved by other visual cues. The criterion should not penalize plausible explanations for why certain elements are missing — only hallucinations or misrepresentations — and should not be applied to answers that are factually inconsistent with the image. When in doubt, the answer that minimizes speculation and maximizes visual fidelity wins — but only if both are factually consistent. The goal is to reward answers that are faithful to the visual record — not stylistically conservative, complete, or vague — and to penalize only hallucinations or contradictions.

current_criteria.name: specificity
current_criteria.description: Specificity measures the granularity and precision with which an answer describes visually verifiable elements in the image — including object type, color, texture, spatial position, configuration, brand names, labels, or contextual details — but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from specificity evaluation. Specificity rewards answers that add verifiable, non-hallucinated details that enhance visual fidelity — even minor or non-essential elements — as long as they are accurately described and do not misrepresent scale, position, or proportion. It does NOT penalize contextually grounded behavioral or environmental inferences (e.g., ‘waiting for their turn’ from posture, ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window) — as long as they are visually supported and not hallucinated. However, it DOES penalize aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘eye-catching’, ‘visually appealing’) that lacks visual grounding — as these are not descriptive of visual elements but subjective judgments. Specificity does not reward speculative inferences — but does reward inclusion of verifiable, granular details like ‘a browser window’ — even if the action (e.g., ‘browsing’) is inferred. Hallucinations (fabricated objects, actions, or attributes not visible) are always penalized — even if highly detailed — and disqualify the answer from specificity evaluation. Specificity is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent or visually ungrounded answers — those are disqualified before any comparison. It is not about linguistic creativity or detail quantity — it is about precision in describing what is visually present and factually correct. Annotators should prioritize accurate, granular descriptions over vague or generic ones — but only if they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity must not override or compensate for violations of visual grounding or factual consistency — granularity is irrelevant if the answer is hallucinated or misrepresents the visual record. When visual evidence is ambiguous, calibrated uncertainty should be used — not speculative detail — and specificity is not applicable. Examples: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked next to a curb’ is more specific than ‘a red sedan parked’ — both are grounded and factually consistent. ‘A cat with a golden collar’ is penalized — it is a hallucination. ‘A person holding hands with a child’ is rewarded — if the child is visually present. ‘A person with an angry expression’ is penalized — if ‘angry’ is not visually verifiable. ‘A person with a red jacket’ is rewarded — if the jacket is visible. ‘A person with a red jacket that is eye-catching’ is penalized — ‘eye-catching’ is aesthetic and not visually verifiable. ‘A person browsing a web page’ is not penalized — if a browser window is visible — but ‘a person browsing a web page on a laptop’ is rewarded — if the laptop is visible. ‘A person waiting for their turn’ is penalized — if not visually implied — even if plausible. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt’ is rewarded — if the logo is visible — even if not central. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt that says ‘Nike’’ is rewarded — if the text is visible — even if not central. Specificity must not be used to evaluate or override factual consistency — if one answer is factually incorrect, it is always inferior, regardless of specificity. Specificity is not a substitute for accuracy — any factual error or hallucination automatically disqualifies the answer. It is only applicable for factual, visually grounded answers — and does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or non-visual judgments — unless grounded in observable visual cues. The goal is to reward answers that add precision and granularity to the description of visually present elements — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresenting the visual record. Annotators should prioritize verifiable, granular details — even if minor or non-essential — over vague or generic descriptions — as long as they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity is evaluated only after factual consistency and visual grounding are confirmed — and is never applied to hallucinated or factually inconsistent answers.

current_criteria.name: visual_grounding
current_criteria.description: Visual grounding requires that every factual claim in the answer strictly corresponds to what is visibly present in the image — including object identity, spatial relationships, actions, colors, textures, structural support, and quantifiable features — without fabricating, omitting, or misrepresenting visible elements. Annotators must verify each claim against the visual record pixel-by-pixel or via direct observation, not mental reconstruction or inference. Hallucinations — defined as fabricating non-existent visual elements, actions, relationships, or attributes — are always penalized, regardless of aesthetic appeal or contextual plausibility. Misrepresentations — such as misidentifying visible elements (e.g., mistaking a ceiling light for a TV) or omitting clearly visible elements — are also penalized if they misrepresent the visual record. The criterion applies only to factual, observable visual elements — not subjective, aesthetic, or interpretive judgments (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘intriguing’, ‘arrogant’), which are evaluated under other criteria. Visual grounding does not penalize contextually supported inferences (e.g., inferring ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window or ‘on shelves’ from visible shelf structure) — as long as they are grounded in direct visual cues, not speculation. It does not penalize minor aesthetic or stylistic descriptions if they are accurate and do not imply hallucinated attributes. Annotators must report ambiguous elements using calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly a tent’, ‘appears to be’) rather than omitting them. The criterion must not be conflated with factual consistency or specificity — grounding is about fidelity to visual presence, not accuracy of interpretation. When visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer must reflect the ambiguity, not invent or omit. Structural context (e.g., walls, floors, rods, shelves) must be described accurately — even if not central to the question — as they are critical visual elements. Workers must avoid penalizing for plausible inferences, minor misidentifications, or stylized depictions (e.g., ‘bent legs on a statue’) — unless they misrepresent or omit clearly visible elements. The criterion is always evaluated after confirming factual consistency — but only applies to factual, observable visual elements. If an answer contains hallucinations or misrepresents visible elements, it is automatically disqualified from visual grounding evaluation — regardless of other criteria. Visual grounding does not penalize overestimation of counts (e.g., ‘at least twelve’) if the number is visually supported — only if the claim exceeds visible evidence. It does not require pixel-perfect spatial precision — only contextually accurate spatial relationships (e.g., ‘in front of’, ‘behind’, ‘scattered’) — and penalizes only when misrepresentations are visually evident. Composite surfaces (e.g., whiteboards, canvases) and attached items (e.g., sticky notes) must be counted as distinct visual elements. Common or colloquial terms (e.g., ‘water scooter’ for jet ski) are acceptable if they do not misrepresent the object’s core visual identity — and are not hallucinations. The goal is to reward answers that reflect all visually present elements with precision — even if minor or ambiguous — and penalize only hallucinations and omissions of critical visual elements. The criterion is inapplicable to non-living, stylized, or artistic representations unless their visual form is being misrepresented — and does not penalize descriptions of their pose or structure if they are visually present. Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record — and descriptive phrases matching labels are not hallucinations — they are rewarded. The criterion must be applied strictly — no inference beyond what is visually implied is allowed — and must not override factual consistency or other criteria. Examples: ‘A red car with a black roof’ is grounded if the roof is visible; ‘A red car with a black object on top’ is hallucinated if no such object exists; ‘a tent’ is grounded if visually supported; ‘suspended from metal rods’ is preferred over ‘hanging from the ceiling’ if visual support is visible; ‘a person with an open mouth’ is grounded if visible — even if not central. The criterion is always evaluated after confirming factual consistency — but only applies to factual, observable visual elements. If an answer contains hallucinations or misrepresents visible elements, it is automatically disqualified from visual grounding evaluation — regardless of other criteria. Visual grounding does not penalize overestimation of counts (e.g., ‘at least twelve’) if the number is visually supported — only if the claim exceeds visible evidence. It does not require pixel-perfect spatial precision — only contextually accurate spatial relationships (e.g., ‘in front of’, ‘behind’, ‘scattered’) — and penalizes only when misrepresentations are visually evident. Composite surfaces (e.g., whiteboards, canvases) and attached items (e.g., sticky notes) must be counted as distinct visual elements. Common or colloquial terms (e.g., ‘water scooter’ for jet ski) are acceptable if they do not misrepresent the object’s core visual identity — and are not hallucinations. The goal is to reward answers that reflect all visually present elements with precision — even if minor or ambiguous — and penalize only hallucinations and omissions of critical visual elements.

current_criteria.name: visual_stability_and_motion_consistency
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s description of motion, posture, or spatial arrangement is consistent with the visual stability or implied motion in the image — e.g., whether a moving object is described with motion blur, a static object is not described as ‘in motion’, and whether posture implies physical stability or instability. It is applicable only to questions involving motion, implied action, or dynamic scenes (e.g., ‘What is happening?’ or ‘Is this person moving?’). It penalizes contradictions between visual cues (e.g., motion blur) and textual claims (e.g., ‘standing still’) — but does not penalize accurate descriptions of implied motion (e.g., ‘leaning forward’ from posture). It is distinct from ‘temporal_or_action_coherence’ because it focuses on the consistency of visual and textual representations of physical stability or motion — not on sequence or timing. It is also not applicable to static or non-dynamic questions. The criterion rewards answers that respect visual cues of motion or stability — and penalizes over-inference of motion from static postures or vice versa. It is evaluated only after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency — and does not apply to subjective or aesthetic interpretations. For example: describing a person as ‘running’ is penalized if no motion blur or dynamic posture is visible; describing a person as ‘standing’ is penalized if motion blur or dynamic posture is visible. It is not a tiebreaker — only applicable when visual motion or stability is relevant to the question. It does not evaluate the accuracy of motion type (e.g., ‘running’ vs. ‘walking’) — only whether motion is consistent with visual cues. This criterion is distinct from ‘multimodal_coherence’ because it focuses on physical consistency rather than semantic alignment with the image. It also does not apply to non-visual or non-physical descriptions (e.g., ‘calm’, ‘intriguing’).

current_criteria.name: visual_element_hierarchy_and_priority
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer prioritizes the most visually salient or contextually relevant elements in the image — e.g., whether it focuses on the primary subject or action when multiple objects are present — without ignoring critical visual components or overemphasizing irrelevant or background elements. It is applicable only to questions that involve multiple visual elements or a complex scene (e.g., ‘What is happening?’ or ‘Describe the scene’). It penalizes answers that omit the most salient or contextually relevant element (e.g., ignoring the main subject when describing a scene) — but does not penalize omission of less relevant background elements unless they are semantically essential to answering the question. It also penalizes overemphasis on minor or non-central visual details — e.g., describing background objects in excessive detail when the primary subject is the focus. The criterion rewards answers that respect visual hierarchy — prioritizing the most prominent or contextually relevant elements while including only necessary background information. It is evaluated only after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency — and does not apply to questions asking for object identification, spatial arrangement, or non-visual elements. It does not penalize accurate descriptions of minor elements if they are visually present and relevant — but does penalize omission of critical visual components. For example: in a scene with a person and a dog, describing the person is prioritized — but describing the dog is not penalized if it is contextually relevant (e.g., ‘the person is petting the dog’). The criterion is not a tiebreaker — only applicable when visual hierarchy matters. It does not evaluate the accuracy of the visual elements — only their priority and relevance. It also does not apply to aesthetic or subjective interpretations (e.g., ‘calm’, ‘messy’) — which are evaluated under other criteria. This criterion is distinct from ‘completeness’ because it focuses on prioritization — not on inclusion of all visible elements. It is also distinct from ‘specificity’ because it focuses on hierarchy — not on granularity of detail.

current_criteria.name: semantic_alignment_with_question_intent
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s content directly matches the core intent or semantic focus of the question — e.g., whether it addresses what is being asked, without adding extraneous information, omitting key aspects, or misrepresenting the question’s intent. It is applicable to all questions — regardless of visual complexity — and is evaluated after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency. It penalizes answers that misrepresent the question’s intent — e.g., answering ‘What is the person doing?’ with ‘The background is green’ — or that omit key semantic aspects required to answer the question. It also penalizes answers that add non-essential, irrelevant, or contextually unsupported information — e.g., describing the color of a background element when the question asks for object identification. The criterion rewards answers that directly address the question’s semantic focus — e.g., answering ‘What is the person doing?’ with ‘Standing with hands clasped’ — without adding irrelevant details or omitting critical semantic elements. It is not a tiebreaker — only applicable when the question’s intent is ambiguous or when answers are factually consistent but semantically divergent. It does not evaluate the accuracy of the visual elements — only whether the answer’s semantic content aligns with the question’s intent. For example: answering ‘What is the object?’ with ‘a red car’ is semantically aligned — while answering with ‘a red car parked near a green tree’ may be semantically aligned if the question is about the object — but not if the question is about the object’s color. The criterion is distinct from ‘completeness’ because it focuses on semantic alignment — not on inclusion of all visible elements. It is also distinct from ‘specificity’ because it focuses on intent — not on granularity of detail. It does not apply to subjective or aesthetic interpretations — which are evaluated under other criteria. This criterion ensures that answers are focused and relevant — not just visually accurate.

all_criteria.name: visual_grounding
all_criteria.description: The answer must strictly and precisely reflect only what is visually present in the image — including object identity, location, spatial relationships, actions, colors, shapes, and quantifiable features — without inventing, omitting, or misrepresenting visible elements. Annotators must verify each claim against direct visual evidence: if an object is visible, it must be named correctly and positioned accurately; if an object is absent, it must not be claimed to be present. Visual grounding requires fidelity to observable details, including subtle or partially obscured elements (e.g., numbers, logos, textures), and penalizes both hallucinations (adding non-existent details) and false omissions (omitting visible elements that mislead or contradict the image’s content). It does not require minimalism or abstraction — detailed, accurate descriptions are preferred if they are visually supported. Annotators should avoid speculative inferences or structural assumptions not directly visible (e.g., inferring motion or implied structure without visual cues), and should flag uncertainty when visual evidence is ambiguous. The criterion is inapplicable only when the question asks for opinion, interpretation, or subjective judgment — otherwise, visual grounding is always evaluated. Examples: ‘A red car parked on the left’ is grounded; ‘A red car parked’ is insufficient if the left/right is critical; ‘A red car with a black roof’ is grounded if the roof is visible; ‘A red car with a black object on top’ is hallucinated if no such object exists.

all_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
all_criteria.description: The answer must align precisely with the visually verifiable elements present in the image — no fabrication, misidentification, omission of clearly visible elements, or misrepresentation of spatial, structural, or visual attributes is permitted. Annotators evaluate whether every claimed visual detail (objects, positions, colors, textures, labels, spatial relationships, and micro-details) is directly supported by what is visibly present. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., blurry text, partially obscured objects), the answer may express calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly 5 pillows') — but must not fabricate or omit elements that are clearly visible. Omitting visible elements is a factual inconsistency unless those elements are explicitly irrelevant to the question. The criterion applies only to observable, static, geometric, or structural visual cues — motion blur, implied motion, or contextual inferences (e.g., 'warehouse from shelves') are not grounds for factual inconsistency if they do not contradict visible structure. Hallucinations include adding nonexistent objects, misidentifying existing ones, or claiming actions not visually supported — even if plausible. Factual consistency does not require pixel-perfect accuracy or exhaustive detail — only that claims match the visual record. Subjective inferences (e.g., 'calm,' 'arrogant') or aesthetic judgments are not hallucinations unless they imply a fabricated visual attribute. Contextual or inferential claims are permitted if visually plausible and do not contradict the image. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for opinions, interpretations, or non-visual metadata (e.g., artist names, titles). When two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers are applied based on completeness or specificity — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge, and must reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable.' Additionally, the criterion explicitly clarifies: (1) Denying the presence of an object is factually consistent if that object is not visually present; omitting other visible objects is not a factual inconsistency unless those objects are directly relevant to answering the question; (2) Factual consistency is evaluated for each specific claim — not for completeness of the entire scene — and hallucinations (misidentifications) are penalized even if other elements are omitted or inaccurately described; (3) Subjective interpretations of visual arrangement (e.g., 'chaotic spacing', 'orderly formation') are permitted as long as they do not contradict the visible structure — and are not penalized as factual inconsistencies; (4) Factual consistency does not penalize detail accuracy or completeness — only hallucinations, misidentifications, or omissions of clearly visible elements; (5) Visible elements, even if minor or non-central, are essential to factual consistency — and omitting them (especially if they are directly observable) constitutes a factual inconsistency; (6) Factual consistency applies only to visual elements — not titles, artist names, or metadata — and visual elements must be confirmed against the image, not external knowledge; (7) Subjective or stylistic visual attributes (like 'red cheeks') are not hallucinations if they are visually supported; (8) 'Factual consistency' does not apply to non-visual elements — which are evaluated under other criteria — to avoid confusion and misapplication; (9) Relative size or spatial descriptors (e.g., 'small portion,' 'most of the space') are acceptable as long as they are visually accurate — and 'small' does not imply hallucination if the object occupies a portion of the frame; (10) Structural or spatial claims (e.g., 'on shelves' vs. 'hanging from ceiling') must be visually verifiable — and any inference contradicting clear visual structure is a factual inconsistency; (11) Factual consistency requires accurate description of individual visual states when multiple subjects or varying conditions exist — not overgeneralization; (12) Answers must match the specific term requested in the question (e.g., 'English language term'), even if a different term is visually accurate or commonly used — but functional or contextual descriptions are allowed if they are non-visual and non-hallucinated; (13) Factual consistency requires reporting all clearly visible elements — not just avoiding fabrication — and 'unclear' only applies to ambiguous visual cues, not to cases where elements are clearly present but miscounted or misidentified; (14) Omitting visible elements — even if the worker is unsure about their role — is a factual inconsistency, and the number of visible elements must be accurately reported unless explicitly ambiguous (e.g., 'blurry', 'partially obscured'); (15) Adding non-essential, accurate details (e.g., background color, posture, facial expression) is acceptable and does not constitute factual inconsistency; (16) Hallucinations include not only adding nonexistent objects but also misidentifying or misrepresenting visible elements — such as claiming an object is 'revealing his upper body' when the visual evidence shows he is wearing a shirt; (17) Descriptions of visual elements that are inherently stylized, symbolic, or graphic — including implied motion or action — are acceptable as long as they are not hallucinations; (18) Factual consistency does not penalize accurate, non-hallucinated details — even if they are non-essential or redundant — as long as they are visually supported; (19) The criterion explicitly distinguishes between visually verifiable elements and inferred context — penalizing only when inferred claims contradict visual evidence — and must clarify that calibrated uncertainty should not be used to justify unsupported inferences; (20) Factual consistency does not prohibit reasonable, non-hallucinated inferences about behavior, threat, or context — as long as they are grounded in the visible subject’s state and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (21) The criterion must be revised to clarify that 'factual consistency' applies only to observable, structural, or geometric visual cues — not to abstract or interpretive descriptions — and that aesthetic or compositional terms (e.g., 'scattered', 'concentrated') are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual evidence; (22) Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record and must be respected — and factual consistency requires matching claims to all visual cues — including labels, even if they are stylized or child-like — and not just to visual objects or structure; (23) The absence of a label does not imply a claim is hallucinated — and labeled elements must be verified as visually present, not inferred or imagined; (24) If an element is labeled in the image, its description must be factually consistent — even if the label is ambiguous or artistic — and that labels should not be ignored or overruled by other visual cues unless the label contradicts the visual record.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucinated_visual_details
all_criteria.description: The answer must not invent or exaggerate visual details not present in the image. For example, claiming a person is holding a phone when none is visible, or describing a background object that doesn’t exist — such details are considered hallucinations and reduce quality.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question asked. If the question asks about composition, an answer focusing on the animal’s mood is off-topic. Annotators check whether the answer targets the core intent of the question, not tangential or irrelevant information.

all_criteria.name: completeness
all_criteria.description: Completeness is evaluated ONLY for answers that are factually consistent with the image — any answer containing hallucinations, misidentifications, or factual errors is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. Completeness measures whether the answer includes all major, visually verifiable elements that are directly relevant to answering the question’s intent — not every visible detail, but only those whose omission would render the answer incomplete or misleading. Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency before assessing completeness. If an answer is factually consistent, completeness is judged by whether it covers all essential visual components necessary to fully address the question — including object identity, spatial relationships, actions, or contextual elements (e.g., background objects, accessories, or implied states) that are visually present and semantically necessary. Adding non-essential, hallucinated, or speculative details (e.g., inventing a ‘camel’ or ‘legs bent’ not visible) does not improve completeness — it reduces quality. Omitting clearly visible, relevant visual elements (even if not central to the question’s literal wording) is penalized. Examples: If the question asks ‘What is in the foreground?’, omitting a clearly visible object in the foreground is incomplete; if the question asks ‘What is the person doing?’, omitting visible motion or posture is incomplete. Conversely, adding contextually appropriate, visually grounded details (e.g., describing a visible logo or background color) enhances completeness. Completeness does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’ or ‘balanced’) unless they are grounded in observable visual evidence — and even then, they are not required. Completeness is not about verbosity or exhaustive listing — it is about covering only the essential visual components required to fully answer the question. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with more essential, relevant visual elements wins — but only if those elements are visually present and not hallucinated. Completeness is never used to evaluate or override factual consistency — factual consistency is the primary and non-negotiable prerequisite. If an answer is factually inconsistent, it cannot be considered complete, regardless of its detail level. Completeness is evaluated only after factual consistency is confirmed — and only among factually consistent answers. Annotators must reject any answer that contains factual errors for completeness evaluation, and instead evaluate it based on factual consistency first. The criterion does not apply to open-ended, interpretive, or aesthetic questions — in which case, visual grounding and factual consistency are the only evaluation criteria. Completeness should not be used to penalize accurate but non-critical details — e.g., background colors or subtle textures — unless they are essential to answering the question’s intent. If the question does not require object identification or description, then object details are not essential — and omitting them does not constitute incompleteness. The goal is to ensure that factually correct answers are complete in their coverage of the question’s core intent, without over-rewarding detail or penalizing accurate but peripheral descriptions.

all_criteria.name: specificity
all_criteria.description: Specificity measures how precisely and granularly an answer describes visually verifiable elements in the image — such as object type, color, texture, spatial position, configuration, brand names, labels, or contextual details — without introducing hallucinations or factual errors. It is only evaluated when the answer is factually consistent with the image AND visually grounded — and both answers being compared must meet this prerequisite for a valid specificity comparison. Specificity rewards the inclusion of any verifiable, granular detail that is visually present — even if minor, non-essential, or not central to the question — as long as it does not misrepresent scale, position, or proportion. It does not penalize subjective visual descriptors (e.g., 'calm,' 'messy,' 'intriguing') if they are grounded in observable cues (e.g., facial expression, composition) — but penalizes aesthetic or interpretive language that is not visually verifiable (e.g., 'eye-catching,' 'visually appealing'). Specificity does not reward speculative inferences (e.g., 'browsing' inferred from a browser window) — but does reward the inclusion of visually verifiable elements like 'a browser window' — even if the action is inferred. Hallucinations — including fabricated objects, actions, or attributes not visible — are always penalized, even if detailed. Specificity is not a tiebreaker if answers are factually inconsistent or visually ungrounded — such answers are disqualified from all evaluations. It is not about detail quantity or linguistic creativity — it is about precision in describing what is visually present. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding — and if either is violated, specificity is irrelevant. Specificity does not override visual grounding or factual consistency — it is only applicable within the context of factually correct and visually grounded answers. It is not applicable when visual evidence is ambiguous — in which case calibrated uncertainty should be prioritized. Examples: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked next to a curb’ is more specific than ‘a red sedan parked’ — both are grounded and factually consistent. ‘A cat with a golden collar’ is penalized (hallucination) — even if detailed. ‘A person holding hands with a child’ is rewarded — if the child is visually present. ‘A person with an angry expression’ is penalized — if ‘angry’ is subjective and not visually verifiable. ‘A person with a red jacket’ is rewarded — if the jacket is visible. ‘A person with a red jacket that is eye-catching’ is penalized — if ‘eye-catching’ is aesthetic and not visually verifiable. ‘A person browsing a web page’ is not penalized — if a browser window is visible — but ‘a person browsing a web page on a laptop’ is rewarded — if the laptop is visible. ‘A person waiting for their turn’ is penalized — if not visually implied by posture or context — even if plausible. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt’ is rewarded — if the logo is visible — even if it is not central to the question. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt that says ‘Nike’’ is rewarded — if the text is visible — even if not central to the question. Specificity must not be used to evaluate or override factual consistency — if one answer is factually incorrect, it is always inferior, regardless of specificity. Specificity is not a substitute for accuracy — any factual error or hallucination automatically disqualifies the answer from specificity evaluation. It is only applicable for factual, visually grounded answers — and does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or non-visual judgments — unless grounded in observable visual cues. The goal is to reward answers that add precision and granularity to the description of visually present elements — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresenting the visual record. Annotators should prioritize verifiable, granular details — even if minor or non-essential — over vague or generic descriptions — as long as they remain factually consistent and visually grounded.

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
all_criteria.description: The answer should reflect confidence appropriately. If the image is ambiguous, the answer should indicate uncertainty (e.g., “possibly” or “likely”) without overstating certainty. Annotators penalize overconfidence in uncertain situations and reward humility when appropriate.

all_criteria.name: clear_language
all_criteria.description: The answer should be written in simple, grammatically correct, and unambiguous language. Jargon, overly complex phrasing, or unclear syntax reduce clarity and accessibility. Annotators prefer answers that are easy to understand without requiring interpretation.

all_criteria.name: logical_consistency
all_criteria.description: The answer must be internally coherent and free from contradictions. For example, if it says an animal is both “calm” and “in pain,” or that objects are “on opposite sides” while also “centered,” it lacks logical consistency. Annotators evaluate whether the answer’s internal logic aligns with the visual evidence.

all_criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s description of living beings (humans, animals) or their contextual interactions is contextually reasonable and grounded in the visual evidence — but ONLY after the answer has been confirmed to be factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. It does NOT apply to non-living subjects (e.g., statues, logos, abstract art, objects), abstract representations, or spatial arrangements unless they imply biological or physical impossibility (e.g., a giraffe in a cage). Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency — any violation automatically disqualifies the answer from plausibility evaluation. Plausibility is not a tiebreaker or secondary filter — it is strictly a post-verification assessment used to resolve ties between factually consistent, visually grounded answers. It must be based solely on observable visual cues and real-world biological/physical plausibility — no speculation, external knowledge, or aesthetic judgment is permitted. Examples: ‘A dog lying down’ is plausible; ‘A dog singing opera’ is implausible. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., indistinct posture), the answer should remain neutral or descriptive — plausibility judgments are not made. Plausibility rewards interpretations that are contextually reasonable and visually supported — even if detailed — and does not penalize specificity or detail as long as they are grounded. It explicitly excludes evaluative or interpretive claims (e.g., ‘calm,’ ‘arrogant’) unless directly supported by visual cues (e.g., relaxed posture). When in doubt, prefer the answer that makes the fewest speculative assumptions while remaining factually grounded. Plausibility is inapplicable for non-living subjects — such answers are evaluated under other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency). If the criterion is inapplicable, preference must be determined by other applicable criteria — not by defaulting to caution or omitting details. Annotators must never use plausibility to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported inferences — these are penalized under visual grounding and factual consistency. Directional or spatial qualifiers (e.g., ‘toward the left’, ‘extended forward’) are allowed if visually supported — they are not speculative if grounded. Plausibility is not a tool to reward minimalism or penalize contextual detail — it is strictly for rejecting falsehoods in behavior or context. When visual evidence supports an emotional or behavioral inference (e.g., open mouth, raised arms), such terms are not speculative — they are valid under plausibility. Plausibility is not a substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified regardless of plausibility. The criterion is strictly for inferred behavior, not event type or setting — any suggestion of a setting (e.g., ‘stage’, ‘competition’) that contradicts the visual context is a violation. It does not apply to social norms or cultural expectations unless directly supported by visual evidence. Plausibility is never applied to neutral or descriptive observations (e.g., ‘standing with legs apart’) — such observations are always preferred over speculative inferences. The criterion must never be used to evaluate symbolic, stylized, or thematic interpretations (e.g., ‘train-themed’) — these are evaluated under other criteria. Annotators must reject any answer that introduces or misrepresents non-visual or fabricated elements — even if plausible — and must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge. Plausibility is evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and only among answers that meet those prerequisites. If two answers are equally grounded and consistent, plausibility is used to resolve the tie — but only if both are factually correct. Hallucinations (even if plausible) are always penalized — and plausibility is never a tiebreaker if one answer is factually incorrect. The criterion is inapplicable for non-living subjects — and such answers are evaluated under other criteria. If an answer is factually incorrect or visually unsupported, plausibility evaluation is irrelevant — the answer is disqualified. The goal is to ensure that plausibility judgments are contextually reasonable, visually grounded, and do not override factual consistency or visual grounding. Annotators must avoid conflating plausibility with speculation — and must only evaluate it for grounded, factual descriptions of living beings or their actions. Plausibility is not a preference rule — it is a verification filter for contextual reasonableness in living beings only.

all_criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
all_criteria.description: The answer should seamlessly integrate visual and linguistic information — ensuring that the text does not contradict the image and that any implied actions, states, or objects are visually supported. Annotators evaluate whether the answer maintains consistency between what is seen and what is described, even when abstract or inferential language is used.

all_criteria.name: cultural_or_situational_appropriateness
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer avoids culturally inappropriate, socially insensitive, or contextually misleading interpretations — especially when the image contains cultural symbols, social contexts, or implicit social dynamics (e.g., gender roles, religious imagery, or regional stereotypes). Annotators should verify whether the answer respects the visual context without imposing external cultural assumptions, stereotypes, or biased interpretations — even if the visual evidence is neutral or ambiguous. It applies only when the image’s context suggests potential cultural or situational nuance — e.g., a person in traditional attire, a religious symbol, or a culturally specific setting. It does not apply to purely factual, objective descriptions (e.g., object identification or spatial relationships). Annotators should penalize answers that imply or assign inappropriate cultural meanings (e.g., labeling a person’s clothing as ‘slum attire’ or ‘traditional wedding dress’ without context) — even if the description is visually accurate. The criterion rewards culturally neutral, context-sensitive interpretations that avoid stereotyping or misrepresentation. It is not a substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency — those are evaluated first — and only applies when the visual context allows for multiple interpretations. Annotators must avoid penalizing accurate descriptions that are culturally neutral — even if they seem ‘silent’ or ‘passive’ — unless they introduce bias or inappropriate framing.

all_criteria.name: temporal_or_action_coherence
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer correctly describes motion, sequence, or timing that is either visually evident or strongly implied by the image — and only applies when the question explicitly involves dynamic elements (e.g., 'What is happening?', 'Is this person moving?', 'What sequence occurred?'). It does NOT apply to static object descriptions, spatial relationships, or non-temporal questions. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding; if an answer is factually incorrect or visually unsupported, this criterion is inapplicable and should not be used to penalize or reward. Only when the image contains motion cues (e.g., blur, mid-air posture, motion trails), implied sequence (e.g., objects arranged in temporal order), or time-sensitive context (e.g., a clock, action in progress) can this criterion be applied. It penalizes hallucinated or unsupported dynamic claims — e.g., describing a static person as 'jumping' without motion cues — but does NOT penalize plausible inferences grounded in visual state (e.g., 'a browser window implies browsing'). The criterion is inapplicable to abstract art, static compositions, or when the question is purely about object identification or presence/absence. Workers should avoid inferring motion from posture alone or aesthetic terms (e.g., 'dynamic' or 'gestural') unless explicitly supported by visual motion cues. When in doubt, the answer with stronger visual grounding and factual consistency should win — temporal coherence is never a tiebreaker if answers are equally grounded.

all_criteria.name: clarity_of_implied_relationships
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer explicitly or implicitly links visual elements in a way that is unambiguous and logically supported by the image — especially when describing spatial, causal, or functional relationships between objects. For example, if the image shows a person holding a cup, the answer should not ambiguously say 'the person has something in their hand' without specifying the object. Annotators should assess whether implied relationships (e.g., 'the cat is chasing the ball', 'the door is open because the handle is pulled') are grounded in visible evidence and avoid over-speculation. This criterion does not evaluate factual correctness or visual grounding directly — only how clearly relationships are communicated. It is applicable when the question asks about interactions, configurations, or dependencies — e.g., 'What is the relationship between the dog and the ball?', 'Why is the door open?'. If the relationship is visually ambiguous, the answer may use calibrated uncertainty — but if it invents or misrepresents relationships, it fails this criterion.

all_criteria.name: language_coherence_and_fluency
all_criteria.description: This criterion assesses whether the answer’s linguistic structure is grammatically correct, syntactically smooth, and easy to follow — without jarring phrasing, abrupt shifts, or unnatural constructions — even if the content is factually accurate. It focuses on the clarity and flow of the language, not on semantic meaning or visual fidelity. For example, ‘The cat is sitting on a red rug near the window’ is fluent; ‘The cat sitting on a red rug near the window and then the cat jump off’ is less fluent due to awkward phrasing. Annotators should disregard minor grammatical quirks if they do not impede understanding, but penalize convoluted, redundant, or incoherent phrasing that distracts from comprehension. This criterion is especially important for answers that contain multi-part descriptions or complex spatial relationships. It is not applicable to questions that require highly technical or domain-specific language, where stylistic conventions may vary. The goal is to reward answers that are readable and natural to native speakers.

all_criteria.name: absence_of_redundant_or_irrelevant_details
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer includes only necessary, directly relevant visual elements — without adding unnecessary or off-topic details that do not aid in answering the question. Annotators must distinguish between essential information (e.g., object identity, position, color) and extraneous or decorative details (e.g., ‘the background is blurry’, ‘it’s a sunny day’, ‘the image is high resolution’). Redundant details are penalized if they do not add interpretive value, even if they are visually present — e.g., describing the texture of a wall when the question is about object count. Irrelevant details (e.g., describing a person’s clothing in a question about object placement) are also penalized. This criterion is applicable to all questions — especially those with multiple visible elements — and should be evaluated after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency. The goal is to reward concise, focused answers that minimize noise while preserving precision. Annotators should not penalize contextually helpful details unless they are clearly extraneous or misleading.

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty_in_ambiguous_scenes
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer appropriately expresses uncertainty when visual evidence is ambiguous, incomplete, or insufficient — without overcommitting to unsupported claims. Annotators should assess whether the answer uses cautious language (e.g., ‘possibly’, ‘likely’, ‘appears to be’, ‘not clearly visible’) where appropriate, and whether it avoids definitive claims when visual grounding is weak. It is applicable only when the image lacks clear visual cues — e.g., occluded objects, low-resolution details, or ambiguous actions — and not when the answer is factually incorrect or hallucinated. The criterion does not penalize confidence in clearly visible or well-grounded elements — only penalizes overconfidence in ambiguous cases. Annotators should reward answers that acknowledge uncertainty without sacrificing clarity or grounding. This criterion is not a substitute for visual grounding — if the answer is hallucinated, it is penalized regardless of uncertainty expression. It is also not applicable to questions requiring absolute certainty (e.g., object identification in clear images). The goal is to promote responsible, cautious language in visually ambiguous contexts — avoiding both overconfidence and unnecessary vagueness.

manager_prompt:
List and describe 10 criteria for how human annotators compare the quality of two answers to the same visual question.

The task is RLHF-V style preference comparison for visual question answering and image-text responses. The worker model will receive:
- the image,
- the source question,
- candidate answer A,
- candidate answer B.

Focus on human preference factors such as visual grounding, question relevance, factual consistency with the image, avoidance of hallucinated visual details, completeness, specificity, calibrated uncertainty, and clear language.
